# The Task: Major Business Migration

## On Migrations Generally: {.center}

### No one asks the principal agent…

::: {.notes}
No one asks the principal character - the programmer doing the migration.
:::

## The litany of opinions one receives

| Department | Interest |
|---|---|
| Finance | Cost |
| Leadership | Resourcing |
| Tech | Infrastructure |
| Cyber | Security |

::: {.notes}
Risk says the most secure option. Finance says the cheapest. Leadership
says the most supportable, long-term.
Nobody in that room asks the people who will write and read this code
every day what they'd choose.
:::

## I'm trying to install python…

::: {.incremental}
- What is pip, conda, pyenv?
- What's an interpreter?
- What's a path?
- VSCode has python in it right?
:::

::: {.notes}
Cold open, present tense, first person: pip, conda, pyenv — pre-uv world.
What's an interpreter? What's a path? What even is an IDE?
Land the joke — everyone in the room who has installed Python has a
version of this story.
Turn it: the first impression is not a footnote. It sets the tone for
everything that follows.
Note: Don't let this become the whole talk — plenty of talks exist just
on Python packaging. One beat, then move.
:::

## Takeaway: {.center}

### APIs matter.

## Thesis: {.center}

### Choose the easiest thing.

::: {.notes}
Thesis
The hot take: APIs matter more than speed
State it plainly and let the rest of the talk earn it: the API decision
should come first — ahead of performance, cost, and support — because
it's the one factor that determines how much friction the humans on the
team absorb.
:::

# The easy migration

::: {.notes}
I want to outline what goes into an easy migration
:::

## Chapter One: Getting started fast

::: {.incremental}
- Early wins matter
- First impressions matter
:::

::: {.notes}
Pick the API that lets people write real code on day one, before they've
mastered environments, classes, or types.
Imagine you get a cocktail at a new spot, and the cocktail is horrible.
You probably associate this place as not being good, I know so because I
did this. When I went back I got a fantastic cocktail, and I'm a regular
there now. Friction at the start compounds. A team that's writing
working code in week one builds momentum a team still debugging pip
does not.
:::

## Getting Started Fast = "Can I be productive immediately?"

::: {.panel-tabset}
### dplyr

```r
df %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    paid = sum(revenue[status == "paid"])
  )
```

### Polars

```python
df.group_by("group").agg(
    pl.col("revenue").sum(),
    pl.col("revenue")
      .filter(pl.col("status") == "paid")
      .sum()
)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Pillar One: Getting Started Fast
Make this about activation energy and the first 30 minutes/day.
Your selector/aggregation example is good here, but I'd use the simplest
possible version. You don't want to explain the code; you want the
audience to recognize it instantly.

Chapter One: Getting Started Fast
Early wins matter.
First impressions matter.
Pick the API that lets people write real, useful code on day one.
Don't make the first lesson environments, classes, types, or package
management.
Friction at the start compounds.

Then your cocktail analogy works here. The core idea is:
The first experience determines whether people keep going.
The code demo should therefore show "I just learned this and
immediately accomplished something."

The audience takeaway is simply:
"Holy shit, I can already do real work."
Don't get into the philosophy yet.
:::

## Pillar one conclusion: {.center}

### APIs should be treated as customer experience. Treat the consumer like a customer.

::: {.notes}
APIs should be user first, many are, but many aren't.
Frameworks that have user friendly APIs will pay dividends in the
beginning as people come up to speed on the other more complicated
pieces of the language.
:::

## Pillar Two: Keep the same shape of thought

::: {.incremental}
- Easy syntax is a virtue
- Import your philosophy
:::

::: {.notes}
Other options leveraged highly verbose or typed languages, introducing
layers of complexity and friction
We chose Polars because its expression-based API preserved the dplyr
way of thinking about data.
:::

## Code snippet on similarities in syntax/philosophy

`sum(revenue[status == "paid"])` becomes:

```python
pl.col("revenue")
  .filter(pl.col("status") == "paid")
  .sum()
```

::: {.fragment}
**Same thought. Different language.**
:::

::: {.notes}
Pillar Two: Keep the Same Shape of Thought
This should be about transfer, not onboarding.
The question becomes:
After I know how to use it, does the system let me keep thinking about
data the way I already do?
This is where your functional-expression argument belongs.

I'd restructure the points:
Pillar Two: Keep the Same Shape of Thought
Don't make people relearn how to think about data.
Easy syntax is a virtue.
Import the philosophy, not just the syntax.
We wanted an API where operations compose as expressions over columns.
The existing dplyr mental model transfers: select → transform → filter
→ aggregate.
No need to first learn OOP, strong typing, or imperative loops.

Then your selector/conditional aggregation example becomes much more
powerful here than on Pillar One.

Then explicitly call out:
Same thought. Different language.
That's the actual migration story.
:::

## Pillar two conclusion: {.center}

### Some days, you don't need to learn anything new.

::: {.notes}
Asking people to migrate is like information overload, they're going to
learn a ton and it doesn't all have to be at once. Do you take calc 4
before calc 1? No.

When people are comfortable, they'll move on to the fancier stuff and
make more informed decisions.
:::

## Pillar Three: Morale

::: {.incremental}
- Maintain early consistency
- Reduce fear
:::

::: {.notes}
Early consistency improves code sharing and other key abilities, and
increases efforts for collaboration.
By choosing something easy, you can maintain morale and keep people
engaged during what is likely a stressful time
:::

## Maintain Morale → Can the team keep moving without the migration becoming psychologically expensive?

::: {.notes}
Pillar Three: Maintain Morale
I'd phrase the slide roughly like this:
Consistency reduces fear.
Maintain early consistency across the team.
A migration is already disruptive. Don't make every developer's
experience different.
Shared idioms make code easier to read, review, share, and debug.
Early wins build confidence; confidence keeps people engaged.
Choose the tool that lets people feel competent before they feel expert.

I would also change "early consistency"
"Early consistency" is a little ambiguous. It sounds like you're saying
write consistent code immediately, which isn't really the deeper point.

Pillar Three: Reduce Fear
Don't make the migration harder than it already is.
Keep as much of the team's existing mental model as possible.
Shared idioms create consistency in code reviews, debugging, and
collaboration.
Early successes create confidence; confidence creates engagement.
Every unnecessary conceptual change increases the psychological cost of
migration.
:::

## Bring it on home {.center}

### Productivity → Familiarity → Confidence
